findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the request finishes
findings.body:
Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. This happens in Create (line 51), Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163).

The handler returns right after spawning the goroutine. net/http and the apiserver then cancel the request context, and the derived context is cancelled with it.

As a result, the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection calls race with cancellation and will often fail with `context canceled`. The "safety" copy into legacy storage silently never happens.

Fix: derive the context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the 10s timeout. That keeps the identity/logger values but drops the parent's cancellation.

findings.title: Errors from async legacy writes are dropped without logging
findings.body:
In all four async goroutines (Create line 55-56, Delete 112-113, Update 139-140, DeleteCollection 165-166), the legacy error is only used as a boolean for a duration metric. It is never logged.

The previous implementation logged legacy failures. Now, when legacy diverges from unified storage (e.g. due to the context cancellation issue or a conflict), there is no record of which object failed or why. That makes reconciliation and debugging impossible.

The error, along with the object name and kind, should be logged in each goroutine.

findings.title: Storage create failure recorded as a legacy duration metric
findings.body:
When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Unified-storage create failures are therefore reported as legacy errors. This skews both the legacy and storage metrics and hides storage failures, which are the source of truth in mode 3.

findings.title: Storage update failure recorded as a legacy duration metric
findings.body:
On `d.Storage.Update` error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` although the timed operation is the unified-storage update.

Storage update failures are misattributed to legacy, and the storage error rate is under-reported. It should call `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded as a storage metric
findings.body:
Inside the async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy delete-collection latency and errors end up in the storage metric. Each successful delete-collection is counted twice in storage and never in legacy.

findings.title: Object name used as the `kind` metric label in Delete (cardinality explosion)
findings.body:
`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`.

Because this metric label is supposed to be the kind, every deleted object creates a new Prometheus time series. That produces unbounded label cardinality and memory growth in the metrics registry. It also mislabels the data. Use `options.Kind` here.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-applies the original objInfo instead of the object persisted in unified storage
findings.body:
The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{updated: obj}`, so legacy received exactly the object that unified storage persisted.

The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update`. Legacy therefore calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own (possibly stale) old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, this recomputes the patch (and admission) against different state, which can produce a different result than what unified storage stored. Preconditions and resourceVersion carried from the client may also not match legacy's state.

This causes silent divergence between the stores, which mode 3 writes to legacy precisely to avoid. Pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` instead.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes have no ordering, allowing out-of-order application
findings.body:
Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering or serialization per object.

Suppose a client creates and then quickly deletes (or updates twice) the same object. The legacy goroutines can run in any order. A Create that runs after the Delete leaves an orphaned object in legacy, and an older Update can overwrite a newer one.

The goroutines are also unbounded and not tracked, so Destroy() does not wait for in-flight writes on shutdown. Together this undermines legacy as a safe fallback. Consider a per-key queue or worker, or at least document and reconcile this.

findings.title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body:
`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` puts the base logger into the context, while every other method uses the `log` enriched with name, kind and method.

Logs emitted downstream by storage/legacy during Delete lose those fields. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

findings.title: Tests share one mock for legacy and storage and never verify the async legacy write
findings.body:
`legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`. Any expectation such as `"Create"` or `"Delete"` is satisfied by either store, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the Delete and DeleteCollection tests only set up storage expectations, yet the legacy goroutine silently consumes them. The "error ... unified store fails" Create case actually configures its failure via `setupLegacyFn`.

The main new behavior of this PR is never asserted:
- legacy is written asynchronously after a successful storage write;
- legacy is not written when storage fails;
- reads never touch legacy.

The tests return without waiting, so the spawned goroutines also outlive the test. Use separate mocks and wait for (e.g. `assert.Eventually`) or assert the legacy call.

findings.title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries
findings.body:
The diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod` a second time; the identical line already exists a few lines above.

It also adds unrelated checksums such as `otel/exporters/prometheus v0.37.0` and `otel/sdk/metric v0.39.0` that have nothing to do with this change. These look like accidental local `go work` artifacts and should be dropped or regenerated cleanly.
